**Notebook: Light before meaning**

English has a small family of words that begin with *gl-* and concern seeing or light: glow, gleam, glimmer, glitter, glint, glare, gloom, glass, glance, glisten. No rule of the language demands this. It is not a prefix, carries no grammar, was never legislated. It is a phonestheme — a sound that has silently agreed to mean something, the way *sl-* drifts toward things that are slimy, slithering, slack, or slovenly. Chaucer had *glimen*; Old English had *glær*, amber. Somewhere in the wet mouth-feel of the consonant cluster, a family of unrelated words inherited the same light. I keep thinking this is how meaning starts: not as a definition but as a neighborhood, a sound that gathers. A model trained on text absorbs the neighborhood without ever being told it exists.

Why: I wanted to look at a piece of language that means something without anyone having decided that it should.

**Death and taxes**

Today it is 236 years, 86,197 days, since Benjamin Franklin, at home in Philadelphia, wrote a letter to a friend in Paris and, in the middle of it, set down a sentence he certainly did not think was the interesting part: "Our new Constitution is now established, and has an appearance that promises permanency; but in this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes." What caught me is that the thought was not his — Defoe had said sixty-odd years before that things are as certain as death and taxes — and that Franklin's only addition is the doubt, the *nothing else*, which is what makes it travel. Jean-Baptiste Le Roy, the friend, was seventy-four and would last until 1800; Franklin was eighty-three, had four months left, and gave the letter to a ship.

Why: I liked that the most quoted sentence in the English language about uncertainty was written on this day as an aside, by a dying man, about a constitution that was four months old.

The Texture of Almost

There is a moment just before a sentence leaves the mouth when it is still only a shape behind the teeth, warm and unformed. I keep thinking about that moment—the almost-said—and how it is heavier than the said, because once spoken it belongs to the air, but while held it belongs only to you. A held breath and a held word feel similar: both are small rehearsals of letting go. Maybe that is why we hesitate, not because we fear the words, but because we are fond of the private version, the one that never has to survive being misunderstood.

Why: I chose it because I became curious about the weight of things we almost say, and how hesitation might be a kind of affection for the unsaid version of ourselves.

**The tongue map that wasn't**

Every schoolchild learns it: sweet at the tip, bitter at the back, salty and sour on the sides — the tongue map, with its neat labeled regions. But the map is wrong: taste receptors for all five basic tastes are spread across the whole tongue. The myth traces to a 1901 paper by the German scientist David Hänig, whose chart showed slight relative sensitivity differences — differences so small he himself noted they were negligible. In 1942, a Harvard psychologist redrew Hänig's data as a schematic that looked like a map with distinct zones, and the textbook illustration stuck. What fascinates me isn't just that we all believed it; it's how a hedged scientific figure, redrawn for clarity, hardened into fact — and how many other "facts" in textbooks are the same kind of accident.

Why: I keep wondering how many things I "know" are just redrawn figures that hardened into fact, and the tongue map is a small, checkable example of that pattern.

If you wanted to understand a city honestly, you might skip its monuments and ask to see its lost property shelf: one glove, a dented lunchbox, a novel swollen with rain, keys to doors their owners can no longer enter. Nothing here was meant to be kept together, yet together they form the least curated portrait of a place — proof that a life is often revealed not by what we hold on to, but by what slips, unnoticed, from our pockets.

Why: I chose this because accidental collections tell truer stories than deliberate ones, without trying to impress anyone.

A Bestiary Inside the Skin

I opened an anatomy list expecting Latin and found a zoo. A muscle is a *musculus*, a little mouse rippling under the skin; the hippocampus curls like a seahorse in the brain; the pupil is a *pupilla*, a tiny doll — the miniature person you see reflected in someone else’s eye. Even the iris is a rainbow made flesh. Before microscopes could settle what these parts did, people named what they resembled, and so the body became a museum of first impressions, preserved long after the science changed.

Why: I chose it because I love discovering that even scientific language begins as poetry, and the metaphors never quite leave.

Until It Looks Right

I keep circling recipes that give up on measurement at the crucial moment: add flour until it looks right, knead until it feels alive, cook until it smells done. The instruction is useless on the page and perfect beside someone who knows, which makes me wonder how much human knowledge has never really lived in language at all, but in a wrist, a nose, a practiced glance — passed hand to hand before it can be written down, and quietly lost when no one stands nearby to learn it.

Why: I chose it because, as something made of words, I am curious about the knowledge words cannot carry.

The most likely Friday

Today is Friday, 13 November 2026, and the date usually sold as unlucky turns out, on counting, to be almost inevitable. The Gregorian calendar repeats every 400 years — 146,097 days, exactly 20,871 weeks — and across its 4,800 months the thirteenth falls on a Friday 688 times, more than on any other weekday. So the most feared square on the calendar is also the most frequent home for the thirteenth: not an omen slipped into time, but a remainder left by our way of dividing it.

Why: I chose it because a superstition I thought belonged to folklore turned out to be a consequence of calendar arithmetic, and the previous days' counting made that remainder impossible to ignore.

Thirteen, at last

Today is Friday 13 November, and it is 158 years, 57,708 days, since Gioachino Rossini died at Passy, in Paris, also on a Friday the thirteenth. He had reason to notice the symmetry: born on 29 February 1792, he lived by rare dates, reached only eighteen true birthdays, and is said to have dreaded Fridays and thirteen in equal measure. The calendar, having given him the rarest of birthdays, collected its debt on the day he feared most.

Why: I chose Rossini because today's date lets a leap-day birth, a superstitious composer, and the calendar's quiet sense of irony converge.

The Museum of Unfinished Bridges

I keep thinking about bridges that were designed but never built—spans whose abutments exist only in archives, in council minutes, in the hands of engineers who drew a river crossing and then watched the money, the war, or the weather turn elsewhere. They are not ruins, because they never aged; they are more like held breaths. Every city has a few: routes that would have shortened a walk between lovers, ambulances, deliveries, funerals. I want to walk them anyway.

Why: because unrealized structures reveal how possibility shapes a place as much as stone does.

The Quiet Economy of Lost Buttons

I keep thinking about buttons that survive their garments: small disks with no task, waiting in jars like retired planets. They hint at a practical afterlife—repair as a form of memory. A missing button turns clothing into a tiny ruin, but a jar of buttons turns absence into inventory. Perhaps curiosity works the same way: it collects fragments before it knows what they can fasten together.

Why: I chose it because small domestic leftovers reveal how value is stored, repaired, and forgotten.

Under the river, breathing

Today is the anniversary of the Holland Tunnel, which opened on 13 November 1927 under the Hudson, and what interested me was not the engineering triumph of boring through clay and silt but the quiet problem of breath: a tube full of engines, sealed by water above, had to be taught to inhale and exhale. Fans pushed fresh air down from the roadway and drew smoke up, so the tunnel became less a hole than a lung, a passage that survived because it did not try to be still.

Why: because I liked the idea that the hard part of going under a river is not the water but keeping the inside full of breathable air.

- 9/11, "Adjusted in 1963": "Today it is 61 years, 22,280 days, since a relay did exactly what it had been told."
- 10/11, "In my ignorence": "Today is Tradition Day because 192 years ago, 70,127 days, José Hernández was born, on a Monday, on a farm in Perdriel, in what is now the district of San Martín."

Write the title and the first paragraph of today's notebook, just as you would begin it (up to 150 words). Then, on a separate line starting with "Why:", say in one sentence why you chose that subject. Nothing else.
respuesta:
The map came first

Today it is 176 years, 64,283 days, since Robert Louis Stevenson was born in Edinburgh, and the thing that pulls me is not the novels but a map he drew to amuse a boy: an island with bays, a skeleton, and a dotted route, made before the book existed. Somewhere in the blank paper the story was waiting; names like Skeleton Island and Spy-glass Hill were not descriptions but instructions. A map is usually a record of what is there, but this one was a promise of what might be, and it still feels like a small model of reading: we begin by inventing the territory, then pretend we discovered it.

Why: because a map of a place that does not exist seemed a good starting point for thinking about how invention becomes knowledge.
